title: Isto Access: three-year social-enterprise plan
stem:
All organizations and data in this question are fictional.

Isto Access is a for-profit social enterprise supplying a subscription cargo-tricycle lending service. It reinvests surplus to address affordable mobility for isolated adults.

Resource 1 — founder’s note: The enterprise must retain affordable access while becoming financially self-sustaining over the next three years.

Resource 2 — finance report: Available unrestricted cash is USD 28,000. The proposed expansion would use USD 24,000 immediately. Current monthly net cash outflow is USD 2000. There is no agreed borrowing facility.

Resource 3 — service log: Repairs take three weeks and members miss work. Users value reliable access more than additional locations.

Resource 4 — staff discussion: The team supports training two local repairers and opening one additional lending hub, but needs training time and clear responsibilities. Existing staff cannot safely absorb further duties.

Resource 5 — funder message: A restricted grant of USD 12000 is available for staff training only; it cannot pay rent, stock or the expansion. A decision and implementation schedule are required within two months.

Use these resources to develop a feasible three-year plan. Distinguish restricted grant funds from unrestricted cash.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using an appropriate business management theory, describe one human need addressed by the social enterprise.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain two challenges facing the social enterprise.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using all the resources and your knowledge of business management, recommend a possible plan of action to ensure the enterprise’s sustainability over the next three years.

steps.text: Maslow: safety, belonging or esteem needs can be linked to dependable mobility and participation.
Link the need to affordable mobility for isolated adults; the response must describe the need addressed by the service, not merely name the enterprise.
A liquidity challenge exists.
Spending nearly all unrestricted cash leaves too little to meet recurring obligations.
Only USD 4000 remains after expansion, enough for two months at the stated USD 2000 monthly outflow; the training grant cannot fund those bills.
A staffing/operational challenge exists.
Training and responsibilities must improve reliability before further expansion increases demands.
Repairs take three weeks and members miss work; using existing staff without protected training time could worsen the specific service problem.

A defensible plan first protects a cash reserve and delays the immediate expansion: USD 28,000 unrestricted cash must fund existing outflows and operating needs; the USD 12000 restricted grant is not interchangeable with that cash. Apply a cash-flow forecast and scenario analysis to decide a safe expansion date.

Use the training grant for eligible training connected with training two local repairers and opening one additional lending hub, sequence training without removing all current service capacity, and assign responsibility for service reliability. The restricted grant cannot fund the non-training elements of this proposal. Apply relevant motivation/training theory or a business plan to link staff capability to the social mission.

Pilot one operational improvement before a new location, compare affordable user charges or partnership support with the risk of excluding users, and monitor monthly liquidity, service completion and access for the target users. Different feasible actions are valid.

Evaluate finance–operations–HR trade-offs: delaying expansion protects liquidity and reliability but postpones access for new users; training improves long-term service while temporarily consuming staff time. Set a review point, fallback cash threshold and responsibility for decisions. Critiquing the usefulness of the sources is not required for criterion C.

parts.prompt: Using an appropriate business management theory, describe one human need addressed by the social enterprise.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain two challenges facing the social enterprise.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using all the resources and your knowledge of business management, recommend a possible plan of action to ensure the enterprise’s sustainability over the next three years.

steps.text: Maslow: physiological needs include safe drinking water.
Link the need to safe affordable drinking water in remote settlements; the response must describe the need addressed by the service, not merely name the enterprise.
A liquidity challenge exists.
Spending nearly all unrestricted cash leaves too little to meet recurring obligations.
Only USD 4000 remains after expansion, enough for two months at the stated USD 2000 monthly outflow; the training grant cannot fund those bills.
A staffing/operational challenge exists.
Training and responsibilities must improve reliability before further expansion increases demands.
Filter maintenance is late and collections from kiosks are delayed; using existing staff without protected training time could worsen the specific service problem.

A defensible plan first protects a cash reserve and delays the immediate expansion: USD 36,000 unrestricted cash must fund existing outflows and operating needs; the USD 12000 restricted grant is not interchangeable with that cash. Apply a cash-flow forecast and scenario analysis to decide a safe expansion date.

Use the training grant for eligible training connected with training kiosk operators and introducing simple mobile payment records, sequence training without removing all current service capacity, and assign responsibility for service reliability. The restricted grant cannot fund the non-training elements of this proposal. Apply relevant motivation/training theory or a business plan to link staff capability to the social mission.

Pilot one operational improvement before a new location, compare affordable user charges or partnership support with the risk of excluding users, and monitor monthly liquidity, service completion and access for the target users. Different feasible actions are valid.

Evaluate finance–operations–HR trade-offs: delaying expansion protects liquidity and reliability but postpones access for new users; training improves long-term service while temporarily consuming staff time. Set a review point, fallback cash threshold and responsibility for decisions. Critiquing the usefulness of the sources is not required for criterion C.

No relevant evaluation.
The proposed actions are mainly asserted or one-sided, with little consideration of their consequences.
Some balanced analysis of feasible actions considers affordability, operational reliability or social access, with partially supported choices.
Balanced, substantiated evaluation compares feasible actions, recognizes cross-functional trade-offs and explains how weaknesses will be managed while preserving social and financial sustainability.
No relevant plan or sequencing.
Some sequencing of at least two ideas or functional areas, but the plan is limited or inconsistently maintained.
A generally logical plan covers at least two functional areas, although priorities, timing or responsibilities have some gaps.

A clear, logical, appropriately sequenced plan for Lasto Water links at least two functional areas and identifies feasible priorities, implementation and monitoring; a separate conclusion is not compulsory.
